Lecture 1: Models and causality

Wooldridge Chapter 1, pp 1-14

What econometrics is for

  • Testing economic theories and hypotheses
  • Estimating relationships between economic variables
  • Forecasting economic variables
  • Evaluating government and business policy

The central difficulty is that most data are observational, so you need natural experiments to argue for causality. Chapter 1 also names the four data structures: cross-sectional, time series, pooled cross sections, and panel.

From theory to a statistical model

  1. Theory. Which relationship, why you expect it, and which other variables affect it.
  2. Statistical model. Measure the variables, pick a functional form, find variation that acts like an experiment, test size and significance, and check robustness.
  3. Interpret and communicate the results.

Wage equation (job training)

wage hourly wage. educ years of formal education. exper years of workforce experience. training weeks in job training. u everything unobserved that affects wage. is the wage effect of one more week of training. The question is whether it differs from zero and is large enough to justify paying for training.

Crime equation (from Becker's utility-maximization model)

crime a measure of criminal activity. wage wage from legal employment. othinc other income. freqarr frequency of prior arrests. freqconv frequency of conviction. avgsen average sentence length after conviction.

The term collects the unobserved factors. You cannot see it, so you have to make assumptions about it. Those assumptions become the regression assumptions later in the course.

Prediction vs causation

PredictionCausal effect
QuestionGiven , what is the best guess for ?If changes for person and everything else is held fixed, how does change?
IdeaHow varies with Change to , ceteris paribus
  • Individual treatment effect: one person gets an extra year of education. How does their income change?
  • Average treatment effect: a random person (or everyone) gets an extra year. How does average income change?

Causal effects are identified when predictive relationships are tested with a controlled or natural experiment that enforces ceteris paribus, at least on average.

The experimental ideal and its three threats

Randomly assign the treatment so it is independent of everything else that affects the outcome. Fertilizer and crop yield is the clean case: randomize amounts across one-acre plots and land quality and rainfall are held fixed on average.

ThreatWhat goes wrongSlide example
Omitted variablesRelevant factors you do not control for get misattributed to the treatmentLand quality and rainfall in the fertilizer study
SelectionThe people you observe differ from the populationStudents who seek tutoring are highly motivated; observing only public school students in one district when studying returns to education
SimultaneityTreatment and outcome are determined togetherPolice levels and crime; supply and demand determining prices

Lecture 2: Modeling distributions

Wooldridge Appendix B, pp 684-691 and 704-710

A random variable measures a feature of an individual drawn from a population. A probability model gives the relative likelihood of each outcome, which tells you the expected outcome, how variable outcomes are, and which ones would be surprising. Think of a pdf as the histogram from a census of the whole population.

pdf and cdf

Probability density function (pdf)

Discrete: sums to 1

Continuous: integrates to 1

For a continuous variable, is a density, not a probability. Probabilities are areas under it.

Cumulative distribution function (cdf)

Continuous

Discrete

Nondecreasing, and bounded between 0 and 1.

Computing probabilities from the cdf

Quantile function (inverse cdf)

The median is the 50th quantile.

Joint, marginal and conditional distributions

The joint distribution describes two variables at once, like household income and consumption. Marginals and conditionals are two different ways of reducing it.

Joint

Marginal: sum out the other variable

Use sums instead of integrals for discrete variables. Picture turning the joint histogram on its side and adding up the mass in each bin.

Conditional

The distribution of Y among the part of the population with . It is a different function of for each .

Derivation of the conditional pdf

  1. Take the slice of the joint histogram where . It holds only the share of the population, so it does not sum to 1.

  2. Rescale by the share of the population in the slice.

  3. Check that it is a proper distribution.

NameNotationWhat it describes
MarginalOne variable across the whole population
JointBoth variables together
ConditionalOne variable with the other held at a value

Independence

Independence (each line implies the others)

Every slice of the joint histogram has the same shape, so knowing tells you nothing about .

Why it matters

  • Ceteris paribus on average. In a randomized trial, a coin flip assigns drug or placebo, so assignment is independent of everything else that affects the outcome.
  • Sampling. Independent draws each add new information, so information accumulates as n grows.

Where it fails: time series (effects persist), spatial or network samples, grouped treatments (a family that misses a flight together), and selected samples (people who sign up for a study share features the population does not).

Lecture 3: Summarizing distributions

Wooldridge Appendix B, pp 691-704

Full distributions are hard to compare and impossible to plot in more than two dimensions. Summary statistics, called moments when applied to a population, squeeze a distribution into a few numbers.

Expectation: where the distribution sits

Expected value

Discrete

Continuous

The probability-weighted average outcome. It is the balancing point of the distribution and your best guess for if you know nothing else.

Expectation of a function

Functions of two variables need the joint pdf.

Linearity

No independence needed. Expectation is an average, and averages are linear.

Common trap

. In general . Compute as .

Variance: how spread out it is

Variance and standard deviation

Average squared distance from the mean. Units are X squared, so the standard deviation brings you back to the units of X.

Derivation of the shortcut

  1. Expand the square.

  2. Apply linearity.

  3. Use .

Scaling and shifting

Adding a constant does not change variability. Multiplying by multiplies variance by . Only constants have zero variance. Proof: , then square and take expectations.

Standardizing (z-score)

Unitless, so you can compare variables measured in different units, like test scores or neural activation.

Changing slides the curve without changing its width. Changing stretches it, and the variance changes by . A negative flips it but the variance is the same as for . The z-score always has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

Covariance and correlation: how two variables move together

Covariance

Also written . Shared variation. Each joint outcome contributes the product of its deviations from the means, weighted by its probability. Outcomes in the upper right and lower left push covariance up, the other two push it down (slides 23-24).

Derivation of the shortcut

  1. Expand the product inside the expectation.

  2. Apply linearity and use , .

Correlation

Unit-free: the covariance of the standardized variables.

Properties

  • Cauchy-Schwarz: , so
  • Independent implies , because

Common trap

Independence implies zero covariance, but zero covariance does not imply independence. Let be uniform on and . Then , yet is completely determined by . Correlation only measures linear association.

Interactive: covariance as the average signed rectangle

Tap or drag over the points. Each point makes a rectangle from the means to itself. Its area is that point's contribution . Covariance averages them.

Tick "Standardize" and the axes become z-scores: the covariance you read is now the correlation, which is why . The numbers are sample values standing in for the population moments.

Variance of sums

Two variables

The variability of a sum is each piece's variability plus their co-variability, counted twice.

Derivation

  1. Variance is a covariance with itself.

  2. Covariance is linear in each argument, so expand into four terms.

  3. Use and .

Many variables

If the are independent, or just uncorrelated, every cross term is zero and only the variance terms remain. This is the engine behind the standard error in Lecture 4.

Symmetric distributions have skew 0. Normal distributions have kurtosis 3. The slides treat higher moments as minor, as long as they are finite.

Law of Iterated Expectations (LIE)

LIE

Tower property

Average the group averages, weighted by group shares. Conditioning on less information means averaging away the extra conditioning variables.

Sampling and estimators

The population has fixed parameters , such as a mean or variance. You draw a random sample and use it to learn about .

Random sample

Independent: one draw tells you nothing about another. Identically distributed: every draw comes from the same population. Before sampling, each is a random variable. After sampling, the data are numbers.

Slides 17-18 draw incomes from a lognormal population with mean 75 and standard deviation 25. Every sample gives a different histogram, and larger samples give a better one.

Derivation

  2. Pull out the constant, using .

  3. Independent draws have zero cross-covariances, so variances add.

  4. Every draw has variance .

The variance shrinks to zero as grows, which is why the sample average tightens around . Halving the standard error takes four times the data. With the slides' population ():

Bias and variance are separate ideas

Unbiasedness is about the center of the sampling distribution. The standard error is about its spread. Using only is also unbiased for , but its variance is no matter how large gets.

Lecture 5: Inference and hypothesis testing

Wooldridge Appendix C, pp 727-743 (syllabus: Review of Statistics II). Based on Lecture 5, slides 3-33.

Lecture 4 tells us how estimates vary across samples. Lecture 5 uses that sampling distribution to quantify uncertainty and test claims about the population.

How to read the formulas

Hover over a symbol, or focus it with Tab, to see its meaning. Lowercase letters are observed sample values; uppercase letters usually represent random variables before the sample is drawn.

Keep the three spreads separate

QuantityFormulaWhat varies?
Population standard deviationIndividual observations in the population.
Sample standard deviationObserved values within a sample; estimates .
Standard error of the mean, estimated by Sample means across repeated independent samples.

For iid sampling, and (slides 3-8). More data makes the mean more precise; it does not make individuals more alike. Revisit the Lecture 4 sampling simulation to see this distinction.

When is this useful?

Use to describe how spread out your observed data are. Use when your question is about the uncertainty in the sample mean, such as estimating average wages from a survey.

Consistency and the Law of Large Numbers

Consistency (slide 12)

For every fixed , the chance of missing the target by more than that amount goes to zero as the sample grows. We also write .

LLN and continuous mapping (slide 14)

The lecture assumes iid observations with finite variance for the LLN. The mapping must be continuous at the limit. Probability limits add and multiply; they divide when the denominator's limit is nonzero.

Derivation: sample variance and standard deviation are consistent (slide 16)

  1. Rewrite the sample variance.

  2. Apply LLN to the first and second moments, then continuous mapping. The slide assumes a finite fourth moment to apply its finite-variance LLN to .

  3. Take the continuous square root.

Unbiasedness and consistency answer different questions

Unbiasedness concerns the expectation at a given sample size. Consistency concerns concentration as grows. Using alone is unbiased for but generally inconsistent. Dividing the sum of squared deviations by gives a biased yet consistent variance estimator.

Clarification of slide 13: bias tending to zero together with variance tending to zero is a sufficient condition for consistency, by mean-squared error and Chebyshev's inequality. These are not necessary conditions in full generality; convergence in probability alone does not guarantee convergence of moments.

Central Limit Theorem: concentration versus shape

CLT for an iid sample mean (slide 19)

Assume . LLN says the mean concentrates around . CLT describes the approximately normal shape of its standardized error. It does not say the individual observations become normal.

The lognormal income example has mean 75 and standard deviation 25. At , the mean's standard error is 2.5; at , it is 1.25. Quadrupling sample size halves the standard error. Slides 15 and 20 show both concentration and reduced skewness.

When is the CLT useful?

Use it when the population is not normal or its exact sampling distribution is hard to derive, but the sample is large enough for an approximation. It lets you use normal critical values to build intervals and tests for averages.

For , write . The upper-tail probability is (slide 21). Normal approximations can be poor in small, skewed samples (slide 10).

  1. The central 95% of a standard normal lies between -1.96 and 1.96. Use the large-sample approximation with estimated standard error.

Worked example (added): estimating household income

Suppose , and , measured in thousands of dollars. The estimated standard error is .

The slides' two-sigma shortcut gives . These are intervals for the population mean, not intervals containing 95% of household incomes.

What 95% confidence means

Across repeated samples, about 95% of intervals made this way contain the fixed population mean. After observing the data, the interval either contains the mean or it does not. The estimate is always at its own interval's center; coverage concerns the unknown parameter (clarifying slides 24-25).

Hypothesis tests: null, alternative, statistic, decision

Slide 27 tests the claim . Choose an alternative and significance level before examining the result: , , or .

Test statistic (slide 29)

How many estimated standard errors separate your estimate from the null value? Under , the statistic is approximately in large samples.

AlternativeNormal-approximation p-valueReject at 5% when

Critical values above are rounded. The p-value is the probability, assuming the null is true, of a statistic at least as extreme in the direction(s) of the chosen alternative. Reject if ; otherwise fail to reject. A p-value is not the probability that the null is true, nor the probability your specific decision is mistaken.

Which formula should I use?

Worked example continued: test a mean of 70

Two-sided: , so reject at 5% but not at 1%. Upper-sided: , so reject at 5%. Lower-sided: , so fail to reject; the estimate points in the opposite direction.

The 95% normal interval excludes 70, agreeing with the two-sided 5% test. Use matching critical values for this equivalence: the rounded two-sigma interval can differ at the boundary.

Errors, significance and power

DecisionNull is trueNull is false
RejectType I errorCorrect; probability is power
Fail to rejectCorrectType II error

The significance level controls the rejection probability under the null (approximately for an asymptotic test). Power is , where is the Type II error probability at a specified alternative. It depends on the true effect, sample size, variability, and test direction (slides 28, 31-32). Confidence level is , not .

For the slides' true mean of 75, a test of 70 gains power with larger samples in the upper-sided and two-sided cases. A lower-sided test looks in the wrong direction. Failing to reject never establishes that the null is true.

Finite-sample refinements

Slide 33 introduces Student's t and the bootstrap. With iid normally distributed observations and unknown variance, the sample-mean statistic follows an exact distribution under the null. Use its critical values and cdf instead of the normal ones. With nonnormal data, estimating the standard error alone does not make a small-sample t-test exact; the lecture's large-sample approximation still needs care. The bootstrap uses resampling to approximate a sampling distribution.

Check yourself: four quick questions
  1. Does LLN make household incomes normal? No. It makes the sample mean converge to the population mean; CLT concerns standardized sampling errors.
  2. If sample size rises from 100 to 400, what happens to standard error? It halves, holding population variability fixed.
  3. Does mean a 4% chance that the null is true? No. It is a tail probability computed under the null.
  4. Does a two-sided 95% interval containing the null imply rejection at 5%? No, for the matching test it implies failure to reject when the null is strictly inside the interval.
Practice set: use the formulas from Lecture 5

  1. LLN. A population mean is 20. Explain what predicts as a survey grows from 25 to 2,500 people.

    Answer: the sample mean should become increasingly close to 20; the probability of a meaningful gap from 20 approaches zero.

  2. CLT. A population has , , and . Find the standard error and the standardized value for .

    Answer: the observed mean is two estimated standard errors above the population mean.

  3. Confidence interval. Using the same sample information, construct an approximate 95% interval for .

    Answer: the repeated-sampling procedure is designed to cover the fixed population mean about 95% of the time.

  4. Hypothesis test. Test against using , , and .

    Answer: the two-sided normal-approximation p-value is about 0.0455, so reject at 5% and report the p-value rather than saying the null is “proven false.”

Inspectdescribe list codebook tabulateMissing values show as . for numeric variables and blank for strings.
Creategenerate replace ... if& and, | or, ! not, == tests equality, = assigns.
Summarizesummarize tabstat x, stats(mean sd sdmean n)Univariate summary statistics.
Correlatecorrelate pwcorr, sigcorrelate drops any row with a missing value (listwise). pwcorr uses all available pairs. Add , covariance to correlate for covariances.
Run codeCtrl+D (Windows) or Shift+Cmd+D (Mac)Runs the selected lines of a do-file.

Common trap: missing values

Stata treats a missing value as larger than any number, so unemplrate>=8 also flags missing rows. Exclude them explicitly:

gen highun = (unemplrate>=8 & unemplrate~=.)

Do-file skeleton

/* Project: what this is about   */
/* Purpose: what this file does  */
/* Author and date               */

version 15
capture log close
cd "/path/to/working/folder"
log using "output.log", replace
clear all
set more off

use "MyDataSet.dta"

* data preparation and analysis here

log close

Comment with * or wrap text in /* */. The goal is a do-file that reproduces the whole analysis, so someone else (or future you) can rerun it.

What to prioritize for Midterm I

In the order I would study them

  1. Zero covariance does not imply independence. Independence does imply zero covariance. Expect this to be tested.
  2. Be able to derive the shortcuts: , , and .
  3. Know where independence is used and where it is not. It removes the cross terms in the variance of a sum. Unbiasedness of needs only linearity.
  4. Practice LIE as a weighted average of group means, and remember that is a random variable.
  5. Keep two distinctions clean: estimator (random) vs estimate (a number), and bias vs variance.
  6. Distinguish LLN from CLT: concentration around the population mean versus the approximately normal shape of standardized sampling error.
  7. Practice inference from start to finish: choose the alternative, calculate standard error and the test statistic, find the correct p-value, and compare it with the significance level.
  8. Interpret uncertainty correctly: confidence intervals cover a fixed parameter across repeated samples; p-values assume the null is true. Know Type I and Type II errors and power.
